analysis.one_liner: Speeds up federal permitting for energy projects and hands states control over fracking and drilling on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote or a single cosponsor, leaving existing environmental review rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shortened federal environmental reviews of energy projects to two years, required permit decisions within 90 days of a completed review, and given states sole authority over fracking — including on federal land — exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. It would also have locked in 2020 Trump-era rules that narrowed federal water protections, banned agencies from using the social cost of greenhouse gases, extended water pollution permits from five to ten years, and cut the window to sue over an energy permit to 60 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, coal plant operators, and energy project developers. The bill would have sped up federal permitting, capped environmental impact statements at 200 pages, let states take over leasing and regulation of oil, gas, and other energy development on federal land without federal environmental or endangered-species laws applying, codified narrower water protections, restricted EPA's power to veto Army Corps permits after they are issued, eased air pollution permitting rules for plant modifications, and shortened the window for challenging permits in court from years to 60 days.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required all federal agencies to finish authorizations for an energy project within 90 days of a completed environmental review, and set a two-year target for the whole review process.

It would have let states take over leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil, natural gas, and other energy development on federal land, and any state action would have been exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act.
It would have given states sole authority over fracking, including fracking on federal land, in place of federal oversight.

It would have written into law the 2020 Trump-era rules that narrowed the definition of 'waters of the United States,' the 2020 Clean Water Act Section 401 certification rule, and recent Nationwide Permits.
It would have barred federal agencies from using any social cost of greenhouse gas estimates, including the February 2021 interim estimates, in any regulation or guidance.

It would have cut the deadline for filing lawsuits over energy permits to 60 days after the final agency action, with later suits barred, and capped the text of environmental impact statements at 200 pages.

It would have extended Clean Water Act discharge permits from five to ten years, and rewritten Section 404(c) so the EPA Administrator could only block a disposal site before the Army Corps issued a permit.

It would have changed New Source Review rules so that changes at power plants and factories designed to improve reliability or per-unit emissions would not count as modifications requiring modern pollution controls, measured against the highest hourly emissions in the prior ten years.

analysis.who_pays: The public: weaker environmental review of major projects, fracking and energy development on federal land exempt from federal environmental and endangered-species laws, far less time for citizens and communities to challenge permits in court, water pollution permits lasting twice as long between reviews, and federal agencies barred from weighing climate costs in their decisions. People who live near pipelines, wells, and power plants would bear the most direct costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near energy projects; the public

drawbacks.text: Codifying the 2020 rewrite of the National Environmental Policy Act regulations and capping environmental impact statements at 200 pages would have reduced the depth of public environmental review for major projects.

A 60-day deadline for filing any lawsuit over an energy permit, with later suits barred, would have effectively eliminated the ability of affected communities and citizens' groups to challenge permits they learned about late.

State control of energy development on federal land, exempt from the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, would have removed federal checks on drilling and development on land owned by all Americans.
Extending water pollution permits from five to ten years would have allowed dischargers to operate under outdated permit conditions for twice as long before review.

Measuring New Source Review emissions changes against the single highest hourly rate of the prior ten years would have let aging power plants and factories avoid installing modern pollution controls when they upgrade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster permitting has genuine value, and because the bill defines 'energy project' to cover all energy resources, transmission lines and renewable projects could have benefited too. But the bill pursued speed mainly by locking in weaker rules: codifying the 2020 water and NEPA rules so a future administration could not undo them by regulation, stripping federal environmental and endangered-species laws from energy development on federal land, and cutting court access to 60 days. The savings in time would have flowed to project developers, while the environmental and public-participation costs fell on communities near projects and on the public that owns federal land.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, a vote, or even one cosponsor, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on September 22, 2022, near the end of the two-year session.
The House referred it to four committees at once — Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture — and it was then assigned to three subcommittees.
No cosponsors joined from either party, and no committee ever reported the bill or scheduled it for a vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without any floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing environmental review, water protection, and endangered-species rules stayed in place, and energy developers gained none of the new exemptions. The public's current safeguards were preserved by default; the bill's sponsor got a recorded statement of position but no change in law.

for.name: Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it drew no cosponsors from either party

against.name: Chairs of the four referred committees
against.role: Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; it sat in subcommittee referral from September 2022 until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only support was one Republican sponsor, and no Democrat or additional Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would have handed states sole fracking authority (including on federal land), let states take over federal-land leasing exempt from NEPA and the Endangered Species Act, codified narrower water rules, and cut the window to sue over permits to 60 days. Its gains for developers come directly from removing public environmental safeguards.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and other major emitters
industries.note: The New Source Review changes would have let plants modernize without triggering modern pollution controls, measured against the highest hourly emissions of the prior decade, while discharge permits would run ten years instead of five.

All energy projects, including transmission and renewables, would have gotten a two-year review target, 90-day permit deadlines, cross-agency categorical exclusions, and shorter court deadlines — faster approvals for clean-energy projects but the same weakened review for fossil-fuel ones.
